considered_statement: The severe phenotype is known as Hurler syndrome (MPS IH; OMIM 607014 ), and other forms are classified as attenuated MPS I (Hurler-Scheie syndrome, MPS IH-S, OMIM 607015 ; Scheie syndrome, MPS IS, OMIM 607016 ).
exclusion_reason: the 'severe' descriptor here distinguishes Hurler from the ATTENUATED MPS I forms (Hurler-Scheie, Scheie) -- comparative nosological framing that names where Hurler sits on the MPS I continuum, not an anchored disease-level severity for Hurler's dominant untreated sequela; per the BURDEN_INDEX rule, comparative references to other forms do not anchor an entity's own severity. S not lifted

considered_statement: Clinically, the manifestations of Hurler syndrome may vary widely, presenting a spectrum from mild to severe.
exclusion_reason: a second OA source explicitly predicates WITHIN-ENTITY variability of Hurler syndrome ('may vary widely, presenting a spectrum from mild to severe'); under the BURDEN_INDEX severity-spectrum rule a mild-to-severe range is scored at the [H] midpoint, not at an extreme, so a clean non-spectrum disease-level severe tier is not defensibly isolable for Hurler. S kept at the [H] spectrum midpoint

considered_statement: Clinical phenotypes of PD range from the severe infantile-onset form (IOPD), characterised clinically by cardiomyopathy and hypotonia within the first days to weeks of life, to the late-onset form (LOPD), which involves a more slowly progressive myopathy.
exclusion_reason: the cohort entity is the UMBRELLA Pompe disease / GSD II, and the cited sentence states its progression as an explicit RANGE -- 'from the severe infantile-onset form (IOPD) ... to the late-onset form (LOPD), which involves a more slowly progressive myopathy' (rapid/severe infantile pole to slowly-progressive late-onset pole); a single disease-level progression tier is not defensible for an umbrella that spans both poles. P stays at the [H] spectrum midpoint (0.5), which correctly represents the umbrella

exclusion_reason: the available OA progression statement is specific to the CHRONIC form of HT1 ('insidious onset of the chronic form') and concerns diagnostic delay, not a disease-level untreated-progression magnitude; hereditary tyrosinemia type 1 presents in distinct acute (rapidly progressive, infantile) and chronic (insidious) forms -- a form-dependent spectrum -- and the other OA statements describe NTBC-treated cohorts.
